pages.text: Buying a Train Ticket | National Rail Skip to main content Buying a Ticket Find the best train ticket for you Want to know what ticket types are available, how much they cost, and where and when you can buy and use them? Then read on. Which train ticket is the best choice for me? As a general rule, the earlier you can buy a ticket, the better the price you can get. If you know the date and time you wish to travel, then an Advance ticket will be suitable. For more flexibility, Off-Peak and Super Off-Peak tickets and Anytime tickets will be a better option, as you are not limited to a specific date or train. For more information about getting the most affordable ticket for your journey, see below. Advance tickets These must be bought in advance and are only valid on the date and train specified. They are sold in limited numbers, subject to availability and on a first come, first served basis. You can usually buy an Advance ticket up to 12 weeks ahead of travel, and they are still available until the day of travel on many routes – sometimes up to 10 minutes before departure. They offer a great deal if you know exactly when you want to travel. Find out more about Advance tickets . Off-Peak and Super Off-Peak tickets These good value tickets can be bought at any time and allow you to travel on any permitted train during off-peak hours. If an Off-Peak or Super Off-Peak ticket is available for your journey, journey planners will make them available to purchase. In general, Off-Peak hours begin at 09:30 from Monday to Friday in cities and large towns, and at 09:00 everywhere else.

pages.title: By Land and Sea—17 European Trips From London | National Geographic
pages.description: Whether it’s a short hop across the Channel or an overland expedition to the furthest reaches of Europe, some of the richest travel experiences happen when you skip the flight.
pages.text: By Land and Sea—17 European Trips From London | National Geographic By Oliver Smith Published October 24, 2026 This article was produced by National Geographic Traveller (UK). Today, it’s easier to travel further and faster around Europe than ever before — to board a flight and effectively parachute yourself into a new destination. But by travelling overland, be it by ferry, train or car, on a bike or on foot, you’re able to observe the slow, subtle changes at ground level with every accumulated mile. Overland travel by rail is also easier than it’s ever been, thanks to an ever-expanding network of high-speed and sleeper trains across Europe. You might board a morning Eurostar at London St Pancras International and that same day be joining a midnight crawl of Madrid’s tapas bars or standing beneath Milan’s hulking Duomo as stars twinkle above its white marble facade. Ferries, too, offer perspectives unfamiliar to those at the cruising altitude of an airliner, whether that’s witnessing the green coast of northern Spain unravelling out of the blue horizons of Biscay or seeing Icelandic volcanoes peek over grey North Atlantic waves. DOE supports the development, standardization, and maintenance of calibration facilities for environmental radiation sensors. Radiation standards at the facilities are primarily used to calibrate portable surface gamma-ray survey meters and borehole logging instruments used for uranium and other mineral exploration and remedial action measurements. Standards for calibrating borehole fission neutron devices are also available, but are used infrequently. Radiation standards are constructed of concrete with elevated, uniform concentrations of naturally occurring potassium, uranium, and/or thorium. Pad standards have large, flat surfaces suitable for calibration measurements with portable surface survey meters. Borehole standards are large concrete cylinders with 4.5-inch-diameter test holes. Share sensitive information only on official, secure websites. https://www.nist.gov/calibration-services Standards Calibration services Sign Up to Get NIST News GovDelivery Purchase calibrations Learn more about calibrations NIST on a Chip If you need to measure something, NIST is the go-to place for help. And NIST is also the place to go if you need to calibrate your measuring equipment. In our everyday lives, calibrations are often the little adjustments you may make, for example to make sure the colors of your computer monitor or television are accurate, so it will show photos or videos the way that a filmmaker or photographer intended. But for a scientific measurement laboratory such as NIST, calibrations are a bit different. NIST calibrations determine a relationship between the measurement standard (like the Kibble balance) and that instrument or object (such as a cylindrical metal kilogram mass). By using a world-class reference such as the Kibble balance, calibrations make it possible for a piece of measuring equipment to make the most accurate measurement it can. From MRIs to lasers, NIST's calibration services are part of many aspects of everyday life. Driven from the state generations ago, the predators are staging a comeback—and sparking a new fight over livelihood, identity, and the meaning of the wild. Across the pastures of Northern California, more than 200,000 cattle are under threat as wolves return to their former range. Ranch hand Sam Harper discovers a dead calf near the city of Montague. By Nate Blakeslee Photographs by Aaron Huey Published November 3, 2026 Susan H ar t firs t no t iced the wolves one summer about six years back. They’d pop up in the evenings on the ridges of the ranch she runs with her husband, Blair, whose family has raised cattle near Montague, California, since 1852. The Harts are one of the oldest ranching families in Siskiyou County, an enormous, sparsely populated region of rugged mountains and pristine valleys near the Oregon border. The most frequent visitor Susan saw was a wolf with a distinctive light coat and an injured foreleg that spent a lot of time watching the herd. It was clearly too slow to catch a mule deer, the most common prey animal in the nearby mountains, and Susan was worried that it was just a matter of time before it became bold enough to attack one of her animals. That day came in the fall of 2021, when she and Blair awoke to find a bloodied calf with a huge portion of its hide torn away. Please be considerate of the next visitor, and confine all motorized and mountain bike travel to designated roads and trails. The site provides outdoor recreation opportunities in a non-motorized natural setting for 400,000 to 500,000 visitors annually. The 25-mile trail system winds through the woods, providing year-round recreation opportunities on unpaved trails that link to the adjacent 4,000 acre Far North Bicentennial Park trail network managed by the Municipality of Anchorage Parks and Recreation Division (MoA). Popular activities include walking, running, mountain biking, horseback riding, and wildlife viewing. In the winter, activities include snowshoeing, fat tire biking, skijoring, and cross-country skiing. Illustration by Roche How do scientists know which insects can see color? John Jay Rouse | St. Cloud, Minnesota Much of what we know about which colors insects can see is based on a combination of behavioral studies and understanding the morphology and physiology of the insect eye. The compound eye found in most insects is made up of a few to thousands of individual units called ommatidia, and each ommatidium includes a rhabdom, a transparent structure under the lens, which stores photosensitive pigments known as opsins that are used for detecting colors. The more kinds and combinations of opsins an insect’s rhabdom has, the more colors it can see. Most insects can only see a narrow spectrum of colors, if any at all. With a little planning ahead, you can still enjoy desserts in moderation. The dessert dilemma You've heard the saying, "Life's too short, eat dessert first." With so many delicious options out there, it can be tempting. But living with diabetes can make indulging in your favorite sweet treat a little more complicated.
